power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Background: For young people experiencing loneliness or low community connection, physical activity may support social contact, enjoyment and belonging.
Social prescribing offers a person-centred route to organised sport, exercise, active recreation and less structured movement, but identification or referral does not ensure usability.

Little is known about the individual, relational, school and community conditions that make these opportunities meaningful to the young person, workable within their circumstances and acceptable in their social and emotional context.

Methods: A targeted qualitative content analysis with iterative framework development used data from INcreasing AdolesCent social and community supporT (INACT), a school-based social prescribing programme for pupils experiencing loneliness or low community connection. 38 interviews were screened (12 young people, eight parents/guardians, five school staff and 13 link workers); 37 contained physical-activity material.
These were analysed alongside link-worker records for 163 young people.
Material was charted by activity category, setting, pathway stage, barriers and inclusion or emotionalsafety considerations, then compared across pilot interviews, full-trial interviews and logs.
Three researchers contributed to coding, checking and collective interpretation.

Results: Across interviews and routine records, physical-activity material encompassed organised sport, fitness and exercise, dance and creative movement, outdoor activity, informal movement or active recreation, and other community activities.

Five overlapping areas of work were identified: understanding interests and personal fit; expanding activity options; supporting access and entry; working through practical feasibility and sustainability; and considering inclusion and emotional safety.
These areas were not sequential and could overlap or be revisited.
School settings interacted with family routines, peer cultures and community provision to shape usability.
Logs more often documented named activities, practical actions and spending, whereas interviews provided fuller accounts of confidence, social fit and family constraints.
Pathway stages from discussion and referral to attendance and continuation were not consistently distinguished.
Conclusion: For pupils experiencing loneliness or low community connection, access to a potentially connecting physical activity depended on more than availability or referral.
The framework describes the practical, relational and contextual work involved in moving towards meaningful, workable and acceptable participation.
It locates responsibility across families, schools, providers, services and local infrastructure while keeping young people's preferences and choices central.
The study does not establish that physical activity reduced loneliness, but provides a basis for prospective evaluation of participation, social connection and loneliness outcomes.

Physical activity is a broad umbrella term, encompassing organised sport and exercise as well as active recreation, play, dance and less structured movement (Caspersen et al., 1985; World Health Organization, 2024).
text.formatted: Physical activity is a broad umbrella term, encompassing organised sport and exercise as well as active recreation, play, dance and less structured movement <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Caspersen et al., 1985;</ref> <ref type="bibr">World Health Organization, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Regular physical activity supports the physical health, mental health and development of children and young people, yet most adolescents do not meet recommended activity levels and opportunities to be active remain unequal (World Health Organization, 2024).
text.formatted: Regular physical activity supports the physical health, mental health and development of children and young people, yet most adolescents do not meet recommended activity levels and opportunities to be active remain unequal <ref type="bibr">(World Health Organization, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In England, just 49.1% of children and young people aged 5-16 met the Chief Medical Officers' guideline of an average of at least 60 minutes of activity a day in 2024-25.
Further, these averages are underpinned by inequalities.

For example, there is a marked social gradient in participation rates, with 45% of children from the least affluent families engaging compared to 58% among those from the most affluent (Sport England, 2025).
text.formatted: For example, there is a marked social gradient in participation rates, with 45% of children from the least affluent families engaging compared to 58% among those from the most affluent <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Sport England, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: These inequalities are underpinned by a range of factors including affordability and proximity intersecting with disability, gender, sexuality, ethnicity and access to supportive social networks (Dodd-Reynolds et al., 2024).
text.formatted: These inequalities are underpinned by a range of factors including affordability and proximity intersecting with disability, gender, sexuality, ethnicity and access to supportive social networks <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Dodd-Reynolds et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: For example, marginalised young people have described gendered discomfort in gyms, harassment, bullying, and spaces that were physically or socially inaccessible (Dodd-Reynolds et al., 2024).
text.formatted: For example, marginalised young people have described gendered discomfort in gyms, harassment, bullying, and spaces that were physically or socially inaccessible <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Dodd-Reynolds et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: However, the very diversity of these factors underpinning inequalities provides a challenge when attempting to increase access to physical activity.

Organised sport can support identity and belonging, but formal access does not guarantee meaningful participation when ability expectations, cultural capital or exclusionary practices reproduce disadvantage (Kingsley & Spencer-Cavaliere, 2015; Ríos et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Organised sport can support identity and belonging, but formal access does not guarantee meaningful participation when ability expectations, cultural capital or exclusionary practices reproduce disadvantage <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Kingsley & Spencer-Cavaliere, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Ríos et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The activity itself also matters: one option may feel inviting, while another may feel evaluative, gendered or threatening (Dodd-Reynolds et al., 2024; Ríos et al., 2022).
text.formatted: The activity itself also matters: one option may feel inviting, while another may feel evaluative, gendered or threatening <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Dodd-Reynolds et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Ríos et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Further, some sport and exercise settings make performance visible to peers and invite comparisons by ability, particularly when participation is competitive.

Comments about performance, bullying and gendered expectations may then affect whether a young person feels comfortable or safe taking part (Booth et al., 2024; Dodd-Reynolds et al., 2024; Ríos et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Comments about performance, bullying and gendered expectations may then affect whether a young person feels comfortable or safe taking part <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Booth et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Dodd-Reynolds et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Ríos et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Notably, programmes that have attempted to use standardised interventions to increase access have sometimes replicated some of the same inequalities.

For example, the GoActive school-based trial provided similar physical-activity resources across schools, but pupils aged 13-14 from lower socioeconomic groups engaged less with parts of the intervention (Alliott et al., 2023).
text.formatted: For example, the GoActive school-based trial provided similar physical-activity resources across schools, but pupils aged 13-14 from lower socioeconomic groups engaged less with parts of the intervention <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Alliott et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: These patterns suggest that advice or programme availability alone may be insufficient when practical, social and emotional conditions shape whether young people can take part.
Social prescribing offers one possible response to these challenges.
It connects people with nonclinical community support through a co-produced social prescription (Muhl et al., 2023).
text.formatted: It connects people with nonclinical community support through a co-produced social prescription <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Muhl et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Physical activity is one recognised area of social prescribing, alongside arts and culture, nature-based support, advice and other practical services, and work or volunteering (NHS England, 2023).
text.formatted: Physical activity is one recognised area of social prescribing, alongside arts and culture, nature-based support, advice and other practical services, and work or volunteering <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(NHS England, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: In youth services, link workers can tailor support to what matters to the young person, build a supportive relationship and help them access community resources; this may also involve working with families and other services (Farina et al., 2024; Steffen et al., 2025).
text.formatted: In youth services, link workers can tailor support to what matters to the young person, build a supportive relationship and help them access community resources; this may also involve working with families and other services <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Farina et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Steffen et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Young people have also identified shared decision-making and social support as important to engagement (Olsson et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Young people have also identified shared decision-making and social support as important to engagement <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Olsson et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This person-centred, coordinating role may help address barriers that general advice or programme availability leave untouched, and allow a referral to be targeted to the needs and interests of an individual, but current evidence does not establish that it improves uptake or outcomes.

Existing work on youth social prescribing reports substantial variation in populations, referral routes, linking roles, activities and outcomes, alongside a still-limited evidence base (Bertotti et al., 2022; Muhl et al., 2025; Mitchell et al., 2025), while recent implementation research has focused mainly on how services are configured (Berry et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Existing work on youth social prescribing reports substantial variation in populations, referral routes, linking roles, activities and outcomes, alongside a still-limited evidence base <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bertotti et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Muhl et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Mitchell et al., 2025)</ref>, while recent implementation research has focused mainly on how services are configured <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Berry et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: What remains less clear is whether social prescribing helps to make a particular physical activity opportunity usable.

Here, we define as "usability" as whether an intervention is appropriate or meaningful to an individual and valued by them, feasible in being something they can practically take up, and acceptable in that it is experienced as something that is comfortable, inclusive and emotionally safe (Proctor et al., 2011)  (Sekhon et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Here, we define as "usability" as whether an intervention is appropriate or meaningful to an individual and valued by them, feasible in being something they can practically take up, and acceptable in that it is experienced as something that is comfortable, inclusive and emotionally safe <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Proctor et al., 2011)</ref>  <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Sekhon et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Moving towards usability in the context of youth referrals to physical activity via a social prescribing pathway may require coordination across the young person, family, school and community provider because permission, routines, confidence and unfamiliar settings can all shape access.
School-based delivery may offer a familiar route into support, but an available option can still remain unusable for a particular young person even within this context (Hayes et al., 2025).
text.formatted: School-based delivery may offer a familiar route into support, but an available option can still remain unusable for a particular young person even within this context <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Hayes et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Existing reviews and implementation studies of social prescribing have focused mainly on service configuration, service-level feasibility and acceptability, and broad outcomes, often treating individual community opportunities as one component of a wider pathway (Muhl et al., 2025; Mitchell et al., 2025; Berry et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Existing reviews and implementation studies of social prescribing have focused mainly on service configuration, service-level feasibility and acceptability, and broad outcomes, often treating individual community opportunities as one component of a wider pathway <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Muhl et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Mitchell et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Berry et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Less is therefore known about whether an individual opportunity fits a young person's interests and circumstances, or about the practical and relational work through which it becomes usable or stalls before that point.
INACT is a co-produced, school-based social prescribing programme for pupils experiencing loneliness and low community connection.

In both the pilot and full trial, link workers were based in or worked alongside participating schools, using conversations about 'what matters' to each young person to support connections with community resources (Hayes et al., 2025; Hayes et al., 2026).
text.formatted: In both the pilot and full trial, link workers were based in or worked alongside participating schools, using conversations about 'what matters' to each young person to support connections with community resources <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Hayes et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Hayes et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Schools therefore provided the route into support, while the opportunities discussed could take place in the wider community.
Details of how loneliness and community connection were assessed for trial eligibility are reported in the respective protocols; these measures were not analysed as outcomes in the present study.
For pupils allocated to the social prescribing arm, physical activity was one of several possible topics or community connections, rather than a required referral destination.

We used a matrix-based qualitative content analysis informed by the Framework Method (Gale et al., 2013), combining descriptive classification of physical activity material with analysis of the work involved in making opportunities usable.
text.formatted: We used a matrix-based qualitative content analysis informed by the Framework Method <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Gale et al., 2013)</ref>, combining descriptive classification of physical activity material with analysis of the work involved in making opportunities usable.

text.text: Reporting followed the Standards for Reporting Qualitative Research (O' Brien et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Reporting followed the Standards for Reporting Qualitative Research (O' <ref type="bibr">Brien et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Data came from the INACT pilot and full trial.

The pilot randomised pupils in mainstream English primary and secondary schools to social prescribing, with a dedicated link worker, or signposting through a leaflet mapping the local area; this analysis included only pupils allocated to social prescribing, who received six one-to-one link worker sessions over eight weeks (Hayes et al., 2025).
text.formatted: The pilot randomised pupils in mainstream English primary and secondary schools to social prescribing, with a dedicated link worker, or signposting through a leaflet mapping the local area; this analysis included only pupils allocated to social prescribing, who received six one-to-one link worker sessions over eight weeks <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Hayes et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The full trial retained the school-based, person-centred pathway and expanded evaluation of effectiveness, costeffectiveness and implementation (Hayes et al., 2026).
text.formatted: The full trial retained the school-based, person-centred pathway and expanded evaluation of effectiveness, costeffectiveness and implementation <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Hayes et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: All available de-identified transcripts and populated link worker logs for pupils allocated to social prescribing were screened, rather than preselected for physical activity content.
Pilot interviews were conducted from May to August 2025 and full-trial interviews from May to July 2026; the corpus closed on 28 July 2026.

The interview corpus included eight from the pilot (five young people and three link workers) and 30 from the full trial (seven young people, eight parents/guardians, five school staff and 10 link workers).
Confirmed physical activity material was present in 37 transcripts; one young-person transcript contained no confirmed physical activity material.
Of 163 populated young-person log records, 73 contributed confirmed material and 90 did not.
Potential interview-log overlap could not be deduplicated, so source coverage is reported separately rather than as a combined participant total.
Participant characteristics and the availability of demographic information are summarised in Table 1.

text.text: For interviewed young people, the available records contained school year rather than exact age.

Demographic information was collected through optional self-report, and participants could choose whether and which details to provide.
Data availability therefore varied across participant groups and characteristics.
Demographic information was used descriptively; no demographic subgroup comparisons were undertaken.
INACT researchers conducted remote, role-specific semi-structured interviews in Microsoft Teams, where they were audio-recorded and transcribed.
Interviews lasted approximately 30-60 minutes.

Full-trial guides asked directly about physical activity participation; pilot guides did not, and relevant material arose within broader accounts of experience, barriers, implementation and mechanisms.

Link worker logs did not directly ask about physical activity engagement; they recorded each contact, activity options discussed or identified, onward referrals, use of the £40 enabling grant and support such as provider contact, transport or equipment.
The data therefore combined explicitly elicited full-trial material with secondary use of pilot interviews and routine records.
Each discrete physical activity opportunity, experience, barrier or safety issue formed one unit of analysis.
Separate activities mentioned in the same passage were entered separately.
The eligibility criteria were developed by NQB and RB during initial screening and refined through team discussion.

Eligible material referred to organised sport, fitness/exercise, dance/creative movement, outdoor activity, informal movement/active recreation or another community activity with an explicit movement component.
Material about barriers, inclusion or safety was included only when it related to a confirmed physical activity opportunity or movement-related choice.
General 'activities' and non-movement clubs were excluded unless movement was explicit or the passage was needed to interpret movement-related choice.
The matrix recorded source, named activity, activity category, setting, delivery format, pathway stage, who raised it, barriers, inclusion/safety, an evidence note, coding confidence and queries.

Each entry received one pragmatic primary category: organised sport (structured or rule-based club, team or coached activity, such as football or boxing); fitness/exercise (planned exercise, such as gym activity or running); dance/creative movement; informal movement/active recreation (casual, playful or selfdirected movement, such as trampoline play or bowling); outdoor activity (movement framed mainly as an outdoor or nature-based pursuit, such as horse riding or skate-park activity); or movement-related community activity (broader community opportunities with an explicit movement component).
Movement with insufficient detail about form was coded as unclear.
Setting and delivery format were coded separately; duration, intensity and health-enhancing thresholds were not inferred.
For this analysis, usability was an organising concept rather than a measured outcome.

An opportunity was treated as meaningful when the young person wanted or valued it; workable when practical conditions such as cost, transport, timing and family routines allowed participation; and acceptable when the activity and setting felt comfortable, inclusive and emotionally safe.
These were interpretive categories rather than scored criteria or fixed thresholds.
Inclusion and emotional safety referred to participants' accounts of comfort, welcome, judgement or exclusion; the analysis did not assess providers' formal safeguarding arrangements.

Analysis followed the Framework Method principles of structured charting, iterative framework development and systematic comparison within and across sources (Gale et al., 2013), adapted to this mixed-purpose dataset.

Deductive fields (activity category, setting, pathway stage, barriers and inclusion or emotional safety) were combined with inductively developed areas of work.
We first descriptively coded the material and compared recurrent actions, conditions and experiences within and across sources.
We then moved from classifying activities to identifying the work involved in making an opportunity usable.
Finally, we compared source patterns to distinguish findings from documentation effects.
Candidate areas were combined where they overlapped and tested against declined, discontinued and formally available but exclusionary examples.
Because elicitation differed, the final framework was checked separately against pilot interviews, fulltrial interviews and logs.
The complete subdataset was analysed, with scope defined by the research questions rather than saturation.
Collaborative coding and critical-friend discussion were used to strengthen interpretation rather than to calculate statistical inter-rater reliability (Smith & McGannon, 2018).

text.text: NQB led the initial extraction and development of the candidate framework under RB's supervision, and RB reviewed the developing coding and source material.
Six interviews spanning the different participant types were independently double-coded, with each interview coded by two researchers and RB, NQB and SEC all contributing to this process.
The three researchers discussed coding decisions, differences and candidate areas, returning to the matrix and original sources where needed.
Reflective notes documented assumptions, category development, source effects and contradictory cases and were revisited while the five-area framework and Results were refined.
For the final checks, quotations were compared with the original transcripts, identifiers were removed and source labels were verified.
The final subdataset contained 264 eligible coding entries.
Of the 264 entries, 29 came from young-person interviews, 37 from parent/guardian interviews, 14 from school-staff interviews, 63 from link-worker interviews and 121 from link-worker logs.
These were not unique participants, referrals or attendance episodes, and their frequencies were not interpreted as estimates of prevalence or importance.
The team compared interpretations across researchers and sources, retained ambiguous and contradictory cases, and recorded decisions in the analysis matrix and reflective notes.

Physical activity material appeared across young-person, parent/guardian, school-staff and linkworker interviews and in routine link-worker records.

text.text: Logs more often named providers, purchases and sessions, whereas interviews provided fuller accounts of confidence, social fit, family constraints and uncertainty.
These patterns reflect what the sources documented rather than the prevalence or importance of particular activities or barriers.

Pathway stage was recorded inconsistently: discussion, suggestion and referral were often conflated, while first attendance, repeat attendance, valued participation and discontinuation were unevenly captured.
Referral-to-attendance and continuation rates could therefore not be calculated.
This documentation gap matters because the records could show that support was offered but not consistently whether acceptable and sustained participation followed.
The central distinction was between the activity itself, and the work needed around it.
Football, dance or swimming described what was discussed, not what had to be considered or done to make it usable.
The five overlapping areas were analytic areas, not stages, intervention components or a checklist (Table 2).

text.text: Several could apply at once or be revisited as preferences, circumstances or experience changed.
The framework did not classify opportunities as usable or unusable; it described work that might move them towards being meaningful, workable and acceptable.

All five areas appeared across pilot interviews, full-trial interviews and logs, although interviews captured emotional and social experience more fully, while logs recorded practical actions and spending more consistently.
Across the five areas, young people's interests and confidence interacted with family and peer support, school routines, link-worker practices, provider conditions and local infrastructure.
The framework therefore describes a multilevel process rather than work located solely with the young person or link worker.

text.text: Exploring interests, identity, past experiences and readiness without relying on broad labels such as 'sporty'.
Looking beyond conventional sport to creative, playful, informal, individual and lower-pressure movement.
Supporting access and entry Finding and contacting providers, explaining what to expect, and arranging practical or familiar-peer support where needed.
Considering cost, timing, transport, family routines, local availability and provider reliability together.
Exploring bullying history, competition, accessibility, unfamiliar groups, meaningful participation, and gender or cultural fit.
Physical activity entered the pathway through an existing interest, a valued identity, a previous experience or something the young person wanted to explore.
Link workers described starting with what the young person said they wanted rather than offering a standard menu of activities.
Interests gave link workers a practical starting point for discussing what mattered and finding a relevant opportunity.
"It was definitely getting their voice and seeing what they wanted to do and then going off and finding that activity in their area so it were easier to get to for them."
(Full-trial link worker, LW-F04) A young person's account of dance showed that the link worker's contribution was to help turn an existing interest in dance into an accessible opportunity.
"I was looking for a dance group before and I told [the link worker] and, yeah, he helped me to join … I just like dancing.
It just makes me feel happy."
(Pilot young person, CYP-P01) Existing participation did not necessarily indicate a need for another referral.
Some logs described young people already attending several sports each week, for whom additional sessions would have conflicted with family schedules.

Conversely, broad labels used by parents, school staff or link workers, such as 'sporty' or 'not sporty', obscured differences between competition, solitary exercise, playful movement and activity with trusted peers.
Interest was therefore a starting point for discussion rather than proof of suitability.
Young people's accounts did not support a simple division between those who liked sport and those who did not.
Some resisted formal exercise or competitive sport yet engaged readily in dance, trampoline play, walking, skating, bowling, pool, darts, climbing or movement-based games.
The difference lay less in intensity than in the activity's meaning, social demands and sense of pressure.

"She will do exercise if she doesn't realise it's exercise … ask her to go play on the trampoline for two hours and you've got to drag her in six hours later … ask her to dance for three hours and she'll do it anyway."
(Full-trial parent/guardian, PG-F02) A link worker similarly described a polarised secondary-school culture in which pupils were positioned as either highly athletic or opposed to sport.
For one young person, non-competitive swimming outside school was acceptable partly because it sat outside team hierarchies and familiar peer judgement.
"It just feels like kids were either … really pro-or anti-sport … there's kind of a culture around sport and athleticism, particularly in secondary school, that can be a bit difficult."

(Full-trial link worker, LW-F03) Lower-pressure activities offered a different experience of participation by reducing public comparison, providing a more comfortable social setting or making it easier to join in.
One young person who did not generally like sport nevertheless found table tennis fun because it allowed them to socialise with friends and gradually meet other people.
They also linked the confidence developed in this familiar setting with joining a non-physical after-school business club.
In this account, confidence developed through table tennis appeared to support wider community participation, even though table tennis was not a link worker referral.
"It's fun.
I just get to socialise with people … I don't really like sports in general, but table tennis is, like, a pretty fun sport for me."
(Full-trial young person, CYP-F04) Across these accounts, suitability depended on the relationship between the activity, its setting and the young person's experience, rather than on intensity alone.
A lower-pressure option could still be physically demanding and socially meaningful.

The table-tennis account also shows that a valued opportunity did not have to originate in social prescribing: the young person linked confidence gained in an existing community activity with joining another group.

Link workers described practical and relational support around first access, including identifying provision, contacting providers, explaining what to expect, arranging transport or equipment, using flexible funding and involving a friend or family member.
This could make an opportunity easier to approach, although the data could not show whether it led to attendance or continuation.
"What would make you feel more confident?
… bringing a friend maybe … we can make that happen for you."
(Full-trial link worker, LW-F04)
The young person who joined dance described moving from fear to familiarity after the link worker helped them understand their anxiety.
The young person linked the link worker's support with the unfamiliar setting becoming predictable enough to try.
"He just helped me understand why I was afraid of going … I'm fine because I know everyone now, so I feel comfortable."
(Pilot young person, CYP-P01) Practical support also mattered.
A parent described a grant-funded taxi enabling a skate-park visit, after which the family returned independently.

The young person described the indoor setting as more beginner-friendly than an outdoor concrete park, peer encouragement when attempting a ramp and a new shared interest through which to approach other people.
Logs also recorded equipment, transport and group vouchers used around first access.
Across these examples, payment addressed only one barrier; familiarity, peer support and perceived fit also mattered.
Movement from interest to attendance was not necessarily linear.
Potential activities were filtered through cost, distance, timing, equipment, family routines, parental confidence, religious commitments and local availability.
These conditions interacted.

A free activity could remain inaccessible if it ended after the available collection time, was too far away, conflicted with other responsibilities or required a young person or parent to approach an unfamiliar club without support.
"Them being free or low cost, nearby and accessible … stuff being offered at school or within walking distance is really pretty helpful."
(Full-trial link worker, LW-F03)
One football example had no obvious financial or travel barrier; the obstacle was the family's confidence in contacting a club.
"We never really got anywhere … a bit of nervousness from mum to actually approach clubs … there were no cost barriers, there were no travel barriers; it was just more confidence to approach."
(Full-trial link worker, LW-F07) Provider reliability could prevent an otherwise willing young person from trying an activity.
One young person woke early to attend a before-school fitness club and also tried an after-school track club, but both sessions were cancelled.
They remained open to trying something similar later, indicating that willingness was present even though both available opportunities had fallen through.
"I did end up, like, waking up early and going to the fitness club.
It got cancelled.
And then the other club that I tried to go to also got cancelled."
(Full-trial young person, CYP-F03) Attending once did not mean that participation could continue.
Swimming passes were used for only a few months when families still lacked weekend transport; other activities clashed with existing commitments or family changes.
Flexible funds helped, but could not secure transport, compatible schedules, reliable provision or sustained family capacity.
As one school staff member noted, small discounts did not necessarily make costly activities affordable.
Physical activity settings were not inherently supportive.
Participants described how competition, body-related judgement, bullying, limited playing time, school peer cultures and unfamiliar groups could leave young people feeling exposed.
Previous harm could shape anticipation before a new session, making the choice to attend a judgement about whether an activity was worth the risk of public failure.
Being formally accepted into an activity did not necessarily mean being meaningfully included.
A school staff member described organised sport as potentially 'brutal' and illustrated how being on a team could still involve very little time in meaningful participation.
"If you've only played like two minutes of a game, you're probably not going to want to go back again because you just think it's a bit pointless."
(Full-trial school staff member, SC-F02) Context mattered even without an overtly harmful event.
One young person spoke positively about a new girls-only football group and the people she had met there; another found mixed-gender physical education awkward.
Similar activity labels can therefore conceal very different social experiences.
These accounts indicate that gender and cultural fit cannot be inferred from the activity label alone.
The parent's account of a young person weighing whether she liked an activity enough to risk failing in front of others shows why young people's choice mattered throughout the framework.
The earlier link-worker account of starting with "their voice" and "what they wanted to do" provides another example of choice shaping the work around an opportunity.
However, the options available were limited: one link worker described a "dearth of options" and the need to find the 'closest approximation' to what a young person wanted.
Figure 1 therefore places young people's choice across the five areas while recognising that link workers could not always offer a preferred activity.

This study examined how physical activity opportunities became usable, or failed to do so, within school-based social prescribing for pupils experiencing loneliness or low community connection.

Five overlapping areas of work were identified: understanding interests and personal fit; expanding activity options; supporting access and entry; working through practical feasibility and sustainability; and considering inclusion and emotional safety.
Together, these areas show how individual preferences and confidence interacted with family and peer relationships, school routines, link-worker support, provider practices and local infrastructure.
The findings do not establish that physical activity reduced loneliness.
Instead, they explain how access to a potentially connecting community activity could be enabled or obstructed across these levels.

Previous studies describe youth social prescribing as combining an understanding of a young person's needs with tailored support, respect for their agency, a trusting relationship and help to connect with community services (Farina et al., 2024; Steffen et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Previous studies describe youth social prescribing as combining an understanding of a young person's needs with tailored support, respect for their agency, a trusting relationship and help to connect with community services <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Farina et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Steffen et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The INACT findings build on this research by showing how these forms of support were applied to a specific physical activity opportunity: assessing whether it matched the young person's interests, helping them contact a provider or attend a session, addressing practical barriers, and considering whether the setting felt welcoming and emotionally safe.
INACT identified barriers at several points between initial interest and continued participation.

Costs, transport and timing could prevent access; familiar settings, low confidence and attending alone could make attending for the first time difficult; and provider cancellations, family routines and limited local provision could disrupt attendance or continuation.
Link workers responded by identifying and contacting providers, explaining what to expect, arranging transport or equipment, using flexible funds and involving a friend or family member.
The findings help to explain a pattern observed in standardised programmes such as GoActive.
Young people from lower socioeconomic backgrounds engaged less with some intervention components, even though provision was similar across schools (Alliott et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Young people from lower socioeconomic backgrounds engaged less with some intervention components, even though provision was similar across schools <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Alliott et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: In INACT, even a free activity could remain difficult to use when transport, timing, confidence or the setting made attendance hard.

Providing individualised support to identify and overcome these barriers depended on relevant skills and ongoing support for link workers (Booth et al., 2026), as well as sufficient capacity, local knowledge, provider relationships and flexible resources (Bradbury et al., 2026).

text.text: School-based delivery gave pupils a familiar route to link-worker support and enabled coordination with school staff, but school routines, parental permission processes and peer cultures also shaped what could be offered and how participation felt.
Social prescribing therefore sat alongside existing physical activity provision, adding individual matching and coordination rather than simply providing another activity.

However, the reach of social prescribing still depended on local options; when only the 'closest approximation' was available, it was still possible that the offer could not fully match what the young person wanted.

Similar link-worker functions have been identified in youth social-prescribing services involving arts and other community activities, so these forms of support are not unique to physical activity (Farina et al., 2024; Steffen et al., 2025).

text.text: Young people have similarly emphasised shared decisions, social support and the availability of suitable local opportunities (Olsson et al., 2025).

text.text: Performance and peer judgement may also arise in other group activities.
In INACT, however, the physical activity accounts linked these concerns to specific features of sport and exercise.

A girls-only football group was described positively, whereas mixed-gender physical education felt awkward; being on a team did not feel inclusive when a young person received very little playing time; and previous weight-related bullying made the possibility of failing in front of others feel risky.

These examples show that an activity could match a young person's interests but still feel unsuitable or unwelcoming because of how participation was organised and experienced, particularly after previous bullying or exclusion (Dodd-Reynolds et al., 2024; Ríos et al., 2022).

text.text: Attention to these social experiences of participation was particularly relevant because INACT recruited pupils experiencing loneliness or low community connection.
Reviews suggest that the relationship between physical activity and loneliness depends partly on the social experience of taking part (Pels & Kleinert, 2016; Ahn et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Reviews suggest that the relationship between physical activity and loneliness depends partly on the social experience of taking part <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Pels & Kleinert, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Ahn et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: A setting that reproduced judgement or exclusion could therefore work against the aim of supporting connection.
By contrast, physical activity might support connection when it gave young people a shared focus for conversation and a sense of familiarity and encouragement.
These contrasting experiences show why physical activity referrals required link workers to consider both the activity and how taking part was likely to feel for the young person.

The fifth area of the framework, inclusion and emotional safety, captures this part of usability by focusing on whether a young person feels able and welcome to take part, rather than simply whether an activity has been offered or attended.
The clearest strength of this study was the combination of narrated experience and contemporaneous delivery records.

The analysis included 37 interviews with young people, parents/guardians, school staff and link workers, alongside routine logs for 163 young people, of whom 73 contributed confirmed physical activity material.
Together, these sources captured established participation, new connections, rejected or disrupted opportunities and adverse experiences across varied forms of movement.
Interpretation did not depend on one researcher's reading: three researchers contributed to coding, checking and collective development of the framework, including overlap coding of six transcripts.
Reflective notes preserved how interpretations changed.
The analysis retained uncertain and contradictory examples, including declined, discontinued and exclusionary opportunities, and examined differences between what interviews and logs captured.
Using interviews from four participant groups alongside routine logs allowed the framework to be checked against narrated experiences, delivery records and unsuccessful referrals.
The principal limitations concern what can be inferred from the source material.
The study used a mixed-purpose dataset: full-trial interviews asked directly about physical activity, whereas pilot interviews and routine logs did not.
All five areas appeared across the three source groups, but richer interview detail may still have shaped how they were interpreted.
Coded entries were not independent participants or events, and their frequencies describe extracted material rather than prevalence, importance or effect.
The available data did not allow us to examine whether the opportunities or support documented differed by disability, neurodivergence, gender, ethnicity, deprivation or geography.
As a result, the analysis cannot determine how often or intensely young people were active, causal effects, or whether particular forms of matching or support improved loneliness or other outcomes.
Finally, INACT recruited pupils experiencing loneliness and low community connection.
The five areas may also be relevant to young people referred for other reasons, but their content or relative importance may differ.
Transferability beyond this population should therefore be tested rather than assumed.

Prospective studies should record referral and attendance stages consistently, examine whether opportunities and support differ between groups, and test whether particular forms of support are associated with participation or loneliness outcomes.
Marked inequalities remain in young people's access to physical activity and community resources.

For pupils experiencing loneliness or low community connection, a physical activity referral may provide a route towards social contact, enjoyment and belonging, but availability alone does not make an opportunity usable.

The findings show how young people's interests and confidence interacted with family and peer support, school routines, link-worker practices, provider reliability and local infrastructure between referral and participation.

Link workers could address some barriers through personalised exploration, practical support and supported introductions, but they could not compensate fully for inaccessible, unsuitable or limited local provision.
The study does not show that physical activity reduced loneliness.
Rather, it identifies multilevel conditions that may determine whether young people can access and sustain participation in potentially connecting community activities.
Future research should test whether addressing these conditions improves participation, social connection and loneliness outcomes.

It may depend simultaneously on the young person's interests and confidence, family and peer relationships, school routines, link-worker support, provider practices and the availability of suitable local infrastructure.

To address this gap, the current study drew on data from INACT (INcreasing Adolescent social and Community supporT), a pilot and full trial of school-based social prescribing for pupils experiencing loneliness or low community connection.
It examined how individual, relational, school, service and community conditions shaped whether physical activity opportunities became usable for these pupils.

It asked: (1) what forms of physical activity were documented in the INACT interview and link-worker log data; (2) what work was undertaken to identify suitable opportunities and support access, entry and continued participation; and (3) what practical, social and emotional conditions shaped whether an opportunity was meaningful, workable and acceptable to a young person?
